clue.text: Wedge hammered in restricts small moving part

indicators.note: to restrict something is to keep it hemmed in, and a word hemming another in between its letters is doing just that

parts.note: a piton is the metal wedge a climber hammers into a rock face
S is the clothes-label abbreviation for small

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like carpentry. The wedge is a climber's peg, and once that is seen the clue moves from the workshop to the engine.
explanation.definitionFit: moving part -> PISTON: the piston is the part that slides up and down inside an engine cylinder, turning the crankshaft.

clue.text: Receiving contrary tip, friend had flutter

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so the friend-and-had letters take in the reversed word

parts.note: a pal is a friend
had, as in had a meal, means ate

indicators.note: contrary means turned the other way, so the word is read backwards

explanation.surface: A friend gets a tip that goes against them and has a flutter, a small bet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contrary' turns TIP into PIT, and 'Receiving' puts PIT between PAL and ATE. 'flutter' looks like a bet, which suits the tip, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To palpitate is to beat rapidly or flutter, as a nervous heart does.

clue.text: Group given lift in Transit up to HS2's trackside event

indicators.note: a group of letters given a lift is carried upwards, and a down entry read upwards runs backwards
'in' says the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow, in one unbroken run

parts.note: seven consecutive letters straddle these words, ignoring every space between them, and a down entry reads them from the bottom up

explanation.walkthrough: HS2 is the high-speed rail line, so every word of the surface is about trains. The letters pay no attention to where the words start and stop.
explanation.definitionFit: trackside event -> SHOT PUT: it is a field event, contested on the grass beside the running track rather than on the track itself.

clue.text: Exercise too much without shower in public

indicators.note: 'without' here means lacking rather than outdoors, so the thing it names is missing from the longer word

parts.note: an athlete who exercises too much overtrains
a shower is a spell of rain, and those four letters are the ones that go

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a gym joke about skipping the wash. Only the gym half is real: this shower is weather, not plumbing.
explanation.definitionFit: in public -> OVERT: an overt act is done openly for anyone to see, the opposite of covert, so it is done in public.

clue.text: Worried RAF leaders for instance make fighters stand by

indicators.note: a worried mind keeps nothing in its settled order, so the letters come out rearranged

parts.note: the air force's initials go into the mix exactly as printed

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its head, so only the first of each word is taken

parts.note: the letter at the head of each of these three words joins the pile

explanation.walkthrough: Read straight it is a news bulletin about jittery commanders. In the wordplay only initials survive, and the three they give spell a famous monetary fund.
explanation.definitionFit: stand by -> AFFIRM: to stand by a statement is to declare that it still holds, which is exactly what affirming it does.

clue.text: Anticipate logging area completely

parts.note: trees are felled in a forest, so that is the area where logging happens
'completely' and 'all' swap freely: all in, completely in

explanation.walkthrough: There is no indicator anywhere: the two halves simply sit end to end, which is how the clue gets away with reading as a plain sentence about forestry.
explanation.definitionFit: Anticipate -> FORESTALL: to forestall an objection is to get in ahead of it and head it off, the acting-first sense of anticipate.

clue.text: Heathen has daughter dropped in marked area around bases

indicators.note: the daughter letter D is dropped lower in this down answer, moving two places toward the end

parts.note: an infidel is an unbeliever or heathen

explanation.surface: A pagan whose daughter has fallen into a marked-out field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has daughter dropped' moves the D of INFIDEL, D for daughter, two places down the column, past E and L. The infield is the diamond in baseball and the area near the wicket in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball the infield is the diamond-shaped ground enclosed by the four bases, so it is a marked zone around them.

clue.text: Lay off child who was Home Alone in busy city

indicators.note: 'off' marks a removal: the piece it follows is taken away from the name rather than added to it

parts.note: the boy left behind in that film was played by Macaulay Culkin, and it is his first name that is wanted
these three letters are the ones dismissed, stripped from the end of the name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay off' reads as an instruction to leave the child in peace, which is exactly the film's plot and exactly the wrong sense of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: busy city -> MACAU: the former Portuguese enclave on the Chinese coast is among the most densely packed and least sleepy places on earth.

clue.text: Arranging new pet health insurance, primarily big waste of money

indicators.note: arranging things is putting them into an order of your own choosing, and any order but the given one will do

parts.note: twelve of the thirteen letters, taken exactly as these three words stand

indicators.note: what comes first is what is wanted, so only the opening letter of the word before it is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the policy word supplies the thirteenth

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is household admin, and the join is hidden by 'primarily big': the adverb belongs to the letters before it, not to the size of the waste.
explanation.definitionFit: big waste of money -> WHITE ELEPHANT: the phrase names a possession costing far more to keep than it is worth, and 'big' winks at the beast.

clue.text: Quite good number by singer

indicators.note: 'by' sets two things side by side without saying which leads, and only one of the two orders makes a word

parts.note: an alto is a singer whose voice sits between soprano and tenor
G is the abbreviation for good, as on a school report
read 'number' as one that numbs, with a hard b, and the old anaesthetic answers to it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is the trap, and setters use it constantly: it is never a figure when the surface most wants it to be one.
explanation.definitionFit: Quite -> ALTOGETHER: in 'quite ruined' quite means wholly rather than fairly, and it is that intensifying sense being matched.

clue.text: F1's brand representative?

parts.note: the motor-racing formula is written with this letter, and it is used just as it stands
the one of any suit is the ace

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work. The definition is advertising jargon, and the clue only pretends to be about motorsport.
explanation.definitionFit: brand representative -> FACE: the celebrity hired to front a campaign is called the face of the brand, the public countenance it shows.

clue.text: Floppy alien creature adapted to Klingon, you hear?

definitions.text: creature adapted to Klingon, you hear?

parts.note: something floppy hangs limp
the film alien everyone can name goes by two initials

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is in the definition rather than the wordplay: the Star Trek warrior, heard rather than read, turns into a description of what the creature does to a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: creature adapted to Klingon, you hear? -> LIMPET: said aloud a Klingon is a 'cling-on', and this mollusc clings to rock immovably.

clue.text: Managing debts at university, might one signal bitterness?

indicators.note: to manage a set of things is to handle them into whatever arrangement suits you, and handled letters lose the order they came in

parts.note: seven of the eight letters, taken as these two words stand
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a student in the red. 'At university' is not scene-setting but two more pieces of the mix, one of them abbreviated to a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: might one signal bitterness? -> TASTE BUD: bitter is one of the five basic tastes, and the buds on the tongue are the receptors that report it.

clue.text: E.g. Georgian opposed to what Spaniard says

parts.note: someone opposed to a thing is anti it
the Spanish for 'what' is que, so that is the word a Spaniard would use

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is being sounded out here. The Spaniard is not mispronouncing English, he is simply speaking his own language, and 'says' means no more than that.
explanation.definitionFit: E.g. Georgian -> ANTIQUE: a Georgian chair is one instance of an antique, so the definition works by example rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Sentence of many years cut by one in court, subject to conditions

indicators.note: to cut a word is to slice into it, so what follows lands in the middle rather than alongside

parts.note: a quad is the enclosed courtyard of a college, and it opens up to take the rest

indicators.note: 'in' puts everything assembled so far inside the enclosure named after it

parts.note: the sentence measured in decades is a life one
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' is the trap. The legal one is all over the surface, and the word wanted is the college quadrangle instead.
explanation.definitionFit: subject to conditions -> QUALIFIED: a qualified approval is one hedged about with conditions, a sense quite separate from holding qualifications.

clue.text: Unlikely name for new baby aunt oddly picked at random

indicators.note: 'oddly' picks out the odd-numbered letters, first and third, and throws the even ones away

parts.note: first and third letters of the relative, the even ones discarded
to draw a name out of a hat is to pick it at random

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is topical rather than lexical. It is a perfectly ordinary boy's name, and only a royal scandal has made it an unlikely choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlikely name for new baby -> ANDREW: an everyday British forename that parents have stopped choosing since the disgrace of the duke who bore it.

clue.text: 9 in complete list of Scottish islands

parts.note: a complete list of things leaves out none of them
inch is the Scots word for a small island: Inchcolm, Inchkeith, Inchmarnock

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cross-reference, so 9 across has to be solved first. The wordplay is a single pun: list all those islands and you have listed every Inch.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 -> EVERY INCH: the word at 9 across means wholly and without reservation, and 'every inch a champion' says precisely the same thing.

clue.text: Article on green bananas named botanical types, say

indicators.note: to go bananas is to go out of your mind, and letters out of their mind will not stay in the order they were given

parts.note: the indefinite article is the single letter A
the colour joins the mix whole, all five of its letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Green bananas' is one image on the surface and two separate jobs underneath, the colour being the material and the fruit the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: botanical types, say -> GENERA: a genus is the rank of classification above species, used of animals as well as plants, so botany is one example.

clue.text: Doctor reunited with Newton leaving full of knowledge

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, and tampered letters come out in a different order
what leaves is no longer there, so the letter named departs before anything is shuffled

parts.note: the eight letters of this word are the raw material
N is the symbol for the newton, the SI unit of force, and that is the letter dropped

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a person in a sentence about scientists. It is the instruction, and the scientist is present only to donate a unit of force.
explanation.definitionFit: full of knowledge -> ERUDITE: an erudite scholar is deeply read, so the phrase names learning gathered from books rather than quickness of mind.

clue.text: Cover fastens in case of effervescence

indicators.note: 'in' places the fastening word inside the letters named next, not beside them
a case is what encloses a thing, so the case of a word is its outer shell, first letter and last

parts.note: the first and last letters of the fizzing word, which happen to be the same letter twice
to clip papers together is to fasten them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Case of' is the giveaway once you know it: in a cryptic it never means a box, only the two ends of the word beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cover -> ECLIPSE: when the moon eclipses the sun it covers it from view, so the verb is a plain synonym for blotting out.

clue.text: Wood for cremation almost in centre of mausoleum

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: a pyre is a heap of wood on which a body is burned
amid means in the middle of

explanation.surface: Firewood for a funeral is nearly at the heart of a tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts PYRE to PYR, and AMID, meaning in the centre of, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian pyramids were built as monumental tombs for pharaohs, so a pyramid is a kind of mausoleum.

clue.text: Like meal to be successful?

parts.note: meal is ground grain, as in oatmeal and cornmeal, and so is what a mill turns out
the suffix -ish on the end of a word means rather like that thing: greenish, childish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Like meal' is not a simile but a suffix instruction, which is how a four-word clue manages to be entirely fair.
explanation.definitionFit: to be successful -> FLOURISH: a business that flourishes thrives and grows, so the word covers success of the vigorous, expanding kind.

clue.text: Smallest portion left for banquet's starter

indicators.note: for means in place of, so the word for left stands where the starting letter was
the starter of a word is its first letter, the one being replaced

parts.note: a feast is a banquet

explanation.surface: Only a tiny helping is left of the first course of a big dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: In FEAST, L for left replaces F, the banquet's 'starter'. The surface makes starter a first course; it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The least is the smallest amount possible, so it means the tiniest share or portion.

clue.text: Son asks earnestly for paints straight out of the can

definitions.text: paints straight out of the can

parts.note: S is the genealogist's abbreviation for son
to pray is to ask earnestly, and the third-person -s comes along with it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a boy begging for art supplies. The definition is graffiti, and 'straight out of the can' is what makes it aerosol rather than brushwork.
explanation.definitionFit: paints straight out of the can -> SPRAYS: aerosol paint leaves the can as a fine mist, so the verb names painting done with no brush.

clue.text: Five in comfortable bar save on round of shots

indicators.note: 'in' drops the numeral inside the word rather than setting it alongside
'save' is the preposition meaning except, so whatever follows it is left out

parts.note: the saloon bar of a pub is the comfortable one, with the upholstery and the carpet
these two letters are the ones excepted, and they come off the end
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.walkthrough: 'Save on' reads as thrift and is really a subtraction, which is the disguise the whole clue rests on.
explanation.definitionFit: round of shots -> SALVO: a salvo is a simultaneous discharge of several guns, so shots fired together in one burst is what it names.

clue.text: A little kid awoke, coming round in bed that's dried out

indicators.note: only a small piece of what follows is on offer, and it comes as one unbroken run of the letters already printed there
something that comes round turns to face the other way, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: four letters run consecutively across the gap between these two words, and an across entry reversed reads right to left

explanation.walkthrough: 'That's dried out' sounds like a joke about someone giving up drink. It is geography, and the bed in question is a riverbed.
explanation.definitionFit: bed that's dried out -> WADI: in North Africa and Arabia a wadi is a watercourse that stays empty except after rain, so its bed is dry.

clue.text: Dodgy file naming intelligence operative published in 1950s

indicators.note: a dodgy file is one that has been tampered with, and tampered letters no longer sit in their proper order

parts.note: the ten letters of these two words are the whole of the raw material

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is computer housekeeping. The definition is a biography squeezed into five words, and the date belongs to the novels rather than to the man.
explanation.definitionFit: intelligence operative published in 1950s -> IAN FLEMING: he ran wartime naval intelligence, then began the Bond novels, the first appearing in 1953.

clue.text: Shot, taking aim with it

indicators.note: a word that takes another in swallows it whole, so the second sits inside the first

parts.note: a shot at something is a try, in the have-a-go sense
an end is a purpose or an aim, as in 'to what end?'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' and 'aim' both point at a rifle range and neither is used that way: one is an attempt, the other a purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: with it -> TRENDY: 'with it' is Sixties slang for being in step with current fashion, and the two phrases swap freely in speech.

clue.text: Seat on jumbo had to be turned on using what?

indicators.note: a thing turned round faces the other way, so the word before it is written from the back

parts.note: asking by what means is asking how
the past tense of 'have', its three letters set down from the back

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' looks like one phrase about switches. Splitting it is the step that unlocks the clue, since the closing question is a word in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: Seat on jumbo -> HOWDAH: a howdah is the canopied seat strapped to an elephant's back, and jumbo is the standard crossword elephant.
